name: Gareth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What were you doing at work yesterday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was trying to match a garage's parts invoices to its year-end accounts when the phone kept ringing about tax deadlines. I'm 43, an experienced mid-level accountant at Beacon Tax, about average at the job, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I like a neat ledger and a client who brings the receipts in order; I get tired of fixing somebody else's missing page at the last minute.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens at home when the working day ends, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Selma drives a delivery van, and our children are eight and fourteen; the older one can tell when the mortgage week is close. My pay is lower than most accountants in this role, we have less than a month's expenses saved, and there are few accounting jobs nearby. I don't use AI tools at all; I ask a colleague to show me a result on paper if a system is proposed. I'm not strongly for or against new rules, but I want to see the cost and the person who answers when a return is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the garage owners that a small filing shortcut is fine if the receipt still leads to the right number. I wouldn't make a speech about AI when the missing invoices are the real nuisance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job probably stays, but our pay just covers the mortgage and school costs, and the savings would not carry a missed month. Selma's van hours can vary, so the ordinary household risk is enough to keep me watching bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on matching parts invoices to the bank record with my current spreadsheet and ask the partner for the price of any new sorting service. Starting this month we'd take packed lunches to work and put thirty each week into a mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious despite the quiet technology story. A late wage would be a bigger event than a clever filing button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often are Selma's hours short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parcel firm sometimes cancels a Saturday run when there aren't enough deliveries. We can cover one missing day, but a whole month of gaps would hit the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the sorter yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't used AI and I would leave a test to someone paid to check it. I'd still want to see the receipt against the final figure.

I would ask the partner for the **tool price** before purchase.

Selma’s **variable van hours** already make our bills uneven.

Save **thirty weekly** by carrying packed lunches to work.
feel: He feels **anxious** about an ordinary pay gap and mortgage.

steps.text: Keep matching garage parts invoices against bank records
Save thirty weekly by carrying packed lunches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to say which checks they will remove and whether anyone's hours will change. If a system writes letters to garage owners, someone in the firm still has to read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, writing and answering clients fill my day, and I think the firm will cut one of my paid days when software does more of that. I'm not the fastest accountant here, and less than a month saved leaves no time for a long argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the hours plan in writing and keep handling the accounts I know rather than feeding live files into a tool myself. In the first year of steady change, if my week drops below four paid days, I'd apply for the next posted accounts job at the bus depot and keep any Beacon Tax hours until a written wage offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing part of my own pay. The mortgage needs the full week, not a promise that new work may turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend a software lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm requires a paid demonstration on old files, I would sit beside the senior and watch. I would not run the tool on a client's return without that person checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will school pickup work at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selma could collect our younger child only on days her van route ends before three. I'd ask for a written start time before accepting any depot offer.

I would keep a **human reader** on client letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff that full AGI in 2028 can prepare the accounts and tax returns we sell, so the partners should say who is losing hours. I wouldn't tell a garage owner that a human still checks every line unless someone actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date reaches my desk work; robots around 2031 don't buy me time. I expect my role to end or shrink badly, and Selma's van work may also face robots later, so both wages could be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop paying for the children's weekend cinema trips and save that forty monthly toward the mortgage now. In the first year after 2028, if Beacon Tax ends my post, I'd apply for posted salaried parts-office roles at the repair depots and request mortgage support if eligible while keeping any paid file work the firm offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the household could not carry two wage losses. I can make calls, but I cannot make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are watching films at home for a while until the account holds one mortgage payment. I would keep the small Friday popcorn, because everything cannot be a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move towns for a parts-office role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a written offer gives the wage, start date and enough net pay after travel to keep the mortgage current. I won't move the children for a possible interview.

I would tell clients exactly who **checks returns**.

Selma’s **van job** may face robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the firm show whether garage owners pay for somebody to explain their books, not just print a return. I would want the price written down before anybody calls it a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still have a mortgage, and AGI could do the tax checks I know. Selma's hands-on delivery may face robots around 2034, so five years of wages matter more than talk about a distant future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to let me handle a paid monthly accounts meeting with two existing garage clients, with the firm's fee covering my hours. In the first year after 2031, if both clients renew at that price, I'd stay on the salaried work; if not, I'd apply for posted accounts roles at the depot and keep whatever paid Beacon hours remain until a written offer starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years at least lets us learn if a garage owner pays for a person in the room. We cannot run a household on interest alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you explain at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the owner which unpaid parts invoices are tying up cash and what tax payment is next. If a garage owner says thank you but does not pay again, the meeting is not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners won't fund the meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on ordinary accounts and ask for a written staffing plan instead. I would not do unpaid evenings to prove the idea.

I would require **two renewals** to cover my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to pay down a loan and find out what accounts work garage owners still buy. I don't need a promise that every tax job stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I may still owe on the house, but ten years of full pay could make the debt smaller. AGI reaches my desk in 2036, and robots around 2039 may reach Selma's van route later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add seventy a month to mortgage principal while both wages hold and keep a record of which garage meetings produce repeat fees. In the first year after 2036, if the meeting work covers my salary, I'd stay; otherwise I'd apply for posted salaried depot office roles and take only a written offer with a wage and start time that work for the loan and school pickups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not safe, but I can see the debt shrinking over ten years. A paid job at 53 still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one wage falls before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payment and hold the cash for bills. I would not keep paying principal while groceries go on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our current savings cannot support that. I would rather hold a paid office job as long as I can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a fast cut could arrive before we have one month of mortgage money. A dated staffing answer and a posted role with a written wage would help. I don't need someone to tell me the change is exciting; I need the next pay date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose name goes on a garage owner's return when software fills most of it. The signature is a promise to answer the owner, not a decoration at the bottom.

headlineQuote: The signature is a promise to answer the owner, not a decoration at the bottom.
portrait: Gareth, **43**, is an average-skilled mid-level accountant at Beacon Tax with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
His **low pay**, under-one-month savings and few nearby jobs strain a mortgage shared with Selma and two school-age children.
He **never uses AI**, preferring receipts, prices and a clear person responsible for each return.
He expects **one paid day** lost under steady change and fears a 2028 desk cut most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his wage before the family saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated staffing answer** and a posted job with written wages would let him plan.
